35dfbd067fab: How does the narrator feel about the three shafts in the crater?
Afraid of them and eager to avoid them
He says, “I kept as far away from them as possible, not even venturing to take the faintest peep downwards.”
What does the comparison of the Professor to “a delighted schoolboy” suggest?
He is so excited he loses his usual dignity
He is too young to lead the expedition
He is frightened and wants to go home
He is pretending to be happy for the narrator
He runs “from one to the other like a delighted schoolboy, gesticulating wildly,” showing childlike excitement.
Which contrast does the passage mainly build?
The narrator's fear versus the Professor's joy
The heat of the crater versus the cold sky
The narrator's knowledge versus the Professor's ignorance
The busy volcano versus the empty peak
The narrator will not take “the faintest peep downwards,” while the Professor becomes “breathless and panting” with delight.
ecbbbf4af5f2: What does Sara feel when she sees the ragged child?
Sympathy, because she recognizes the child's hunger
Fear that the child will rob her
Disgust at the child's dirty face
Pride that she is better dressed
“Sara knew they were hungry eyes the moment she saw them, and she felt a sudden sympathy.”
What does the word “forlorn” most nearly mean in this passage?
The child is “more forlorn even than herself,” described as “not much more than a bundle of rags” with “hungry eyes.”
What does Sara's remark that the girl is “hungrier than I am” suggest about Sara?
Sara is hungry herself but thinks of someone worse off
Sara has just eaten a large meal
Sara wants the girl to give her food
Sara thinks hunger is not important
She sighs that the girl “is hungrier than I am,” which shows Sara is also hungry yet still cares for another.
693945988411: What is the speaker's main worry about her marriage?
That it might separate her from her father
That Charles does not truly love her
That her father disapproves of Charles
That she will have to give up reading
She says she would be unhappy “if my marriage were so arranged as that it would part us, even by the length of a few of these streets.”
What does the word “consecrated” most nearly mean here?
She wants her life to be “still consecrated to you,” meaning still given to caring for her father.
What mood does the opening paragraph create?
Quiet and solemn, as if the evening is special
They “had said little,” and the narrator notes “this time was not quite like any other, and nothing could make it so.”
c2cff6bb2b3c: What is Wollstonecraft's central claim in the first paragraph?
Love for humanity grows out of early affection for family
Reason must replace all childhood feelings
Friendship is less noble than family love
Children should avoid playing with animals
She argues few have loved mankind “who did not first love their parents, their brothers, sisters, and even the domestic brutes.”
What does the metaphor “the moral temperature” suggest about youthful sympathies?
They set the warmth or coldness of a person's moral character
They cause children to become physically ill
They measure how intelligent a child is
They make adults forget their childhood
She writes that “The exercise of youthful sympathies forms the moral temperature,” treating feeling like a climate that shapes character.
How does the final sentence qualify her argument for home education?
It admits home education fails if it breeds self-importance
It claims schools always produce better citizens
It says holidays should be made longer
She concedes that if private education “produce self-importance, or insulates a man in his family, the evil is only shifted, not remedied.”
c31a59d08dbf: What is funny about the King's first command to the jury?
He asks for a verdict before any evidence is heard
He forgets the name of the prisoner
He speaks in a language no one understands
He refuses to let the jury speak
The King says “Consider your verdict,” and the Rabbit must interrupt: “There’s a great deal to come before that!”
What does the Hatter's entrance suggest about him?
He cares more about his tea than the serious trial
He is nervous and ready to confess
He is the judge of the trial
He has brought food as evidence
He arrives “with a teacup in one hand and a piece of bread-and-butter in the other” because he “hadn’t quite finished my tea.”
How does the King behave toward the Hatter?
Sternly and unfairly, scolding him at once
Instead of listening, the King snaps, “You ought to have finished,” blaming the Hatter right away.
080ed8752cae: Why is Levin “horror-stricken at his own words”?
He fears he has revealed his feelings too boldly
He has told a lie about his skating
Right after saying “It depends upon you,” he cries, “My God! what have I done!”
What does Levin's need for “violent exercise” suggest about his state of mind?
He is overwhelmed by nervous emotion he must release
He wants to show off to the ladies
He is cold and wants to warm up
He is training for a race
Praying inwardly, he feels “a need of violent exercise” and skates “inner and outer circles,” burning off agitation.
What does the young skater's careless leap down the steps contrast with?
The quiet emptiness of the rink
The young man “dashed down the steps” and skated away “without even changing the position of his hands,” unlike the troubled Levin.
5b5c2e3c9fb9: Why does Anne give Gilbert “a disappointed glance”?
He says he will whip his pupils
He refuses to become a teacher
Gilbert says, “I’ll whip my pupils when they’re naughty,” and Anne is disappointed in him.
Which belief best explains Anne's approach to teaching?
Every child has good in them that a teacher should develop
Reading is more important than character
Anne says, “There is some good in every person if you can find it. It is a teacher’s duty to find and develop it.”
What does Anne think matters most for a teacher?
Influencing children in the right direction
Teaching only reading, writing and arithmetic
She quotes that it is “far more important to influence the children aright than it is even to teach them the three R’s.”
9b890f42da27: Why does Anne want to name the geranium?
Names make things seem more like people to her
She wants to sell the geranium
Marilla asked her to name it
She has forgotten what it is called
Anne says, “I like things to have handles even if they are only geraniums. It makes them seem more like people.”
What does the word “handles” mean in Anne's speech?
She wants “things to have handles,” explaining she means “a name you gave it yourself.”
What trait does Anne show most clearly in this passage?
She imagines the cherry-tree in bloom all year: “one can imagine that it is, can’t one?”
1ef5b4b71123: What is ironic about Jerton's feeling that everyone is staring at him?
He is ordinary and unnoticed, so the idea is groundless
He is a famous actor in disguise
Everyone really is watching him closely
He wants people to look at him
The narrator calls it a “wholly groundless idea,” noting he was “of ordinary appearance, quiet of dress and unobtrusive of manner.”
What does “spuriously interested” mean in the last sentence?
He acts interested in the flower-vase only “to carry off the situation with some appearance of unconcern.”
What effect does the parenthetical “(in imagination)” have?
It shows that the diners are hostile
He is “stared at (in imagination) by several flappers,” reminding readers that the staring exists only in his mind.
02f5d5211d10: What is the narrator's main complaint about these riders?
They treat horses like machines with no feelings
They do not pay enough for rides
They drive too slowly on hills
They think “a horse was something like a steam-engine, only smaller” and drive with “no relief and no consideration.”
What tone is used in “Walk! A good joke indeed!”?
The narrator mocks the riders' attitude: “Oh, no, they have paid to ride, and ride they will!”
Why is the cry “Go along, you lazy beast!” unfair?
The horses are already trying their hardest
The driver is speaking to another man
The road is flat and easy
The horses are “doing our very best to get along, uncomplaining and obedient.”
334caf122539: According to Thoreau, who are the “most serious obstacles to reform”?
Conscientious people who disapprove of the government but still support it
Those who “disapprove of the character and measures of a government, yield to it their allegiance and support” are “the most serious obstacles to reform.”
What is the purpose of the rhetorical questions at the end?
To show that petitioners should act themselves instead of asking the State
To ask the President for advice
To prove the Union cannot be dissolved
He asks, “Why do they not dissolve it themselves,—the union between themselves and the State,—and refuse to pay their quota into its treasury?”
What paradox does the opening sentence present?
The biggest errors depend on good people's virtue to survive
Patriotism has no connection to virtue
Thoreau writes, “The broadest and most prevalent error requires the most disinterested virtue to sustain it.”
550f044ffa1c: What does Raskolnikov's sudden reaction to Zametov's name suggest?
He is alarmed and suspicious about the head clerk
He is pleased to hear of an old friend
He has never heard of anyone named Zametov
He is too sleepy to care
On hearing the name, “Raskolnikov turned round quickly and fixed his eyes on Razumihin.”
How does Razumihin come across in this passage?
Friendly and talkative, unaware of his friend's tension
He chatters, “He is a capital fellow, brother, first-rate,” and asks, “What are you upset about?”
What does Razumihin's qualification “in his own way, of course” imply?
Zametov is likable but has some limitations
Zametov is the best man in the city
He praises Zametov as “first-rate... in his own way, of course,” softening his praise.
5f25175fec0d: What was the main purpose of Boris's plan?
To distract the patron while the narrator slipped out with the suitcase
To win a bet on a bicycle race
To make friends with the patron's wife
To find a job in the hotel
The goal was “to hold the patron's attention for perhaps five seconds, while we could slip past with the suitcase.”
What does the word “reconnoitred” most nearly mean here?
Boris “reconnoitred the stairs” before going down, checking the ground like a scout.
Which details show that the plan's success depended partly on luck and Boris's body?
His big shoulders blocked the office doorway
“The plan might have failed if Boris had been thinner, for his big shoulders blocked the doorway of the office.”
d539c55aed0a: What does the speaker mean by not letting “a little bit of truth check the rush of a big truth”?
Keep an open mind so small facts do not block larger discoveries
Ignore all facts that seem small
Believe only what is already proven
Stop asking questions once one truth is found
He explains, “He meant that we shall have an open mind,” comparing a small truth to “a small rock does a railway truck.”
What is the effect of the simile of the rock and the railway truck?
It shows how a small obstacle can halt something powerful
It shows that truths travel slowly
A small truth can stop a big one “like a small rock does a railway truck.”
How does the teacher feel about his pupil in this passage?
Fond and pleased that he is willing to learn
He says, “Ah, you are my favourite pupil still. It is worth to teach you.”
389f6bc20cde: What does the speaker's halting answer about Mr. Martin's reading suggest?
She is unsure and flustered by the question
She is certain he reads nothing
She is proud of his great learning
She is angry at being asked
She stumbles: “Oh yes!—that is, no—I do not know—but I believe he has read a good deal.”
What attitude does the question “He does not read?” reveal in the questioner?
A tendency to look down on Mr. Martin
She assumes he “is not a man of information beyond the line of his own business,” hinting at snobbery.
What does the gift of the goose suggest about the Martins?
“Mrs. Martin was so very kind as to send Mrs. Goddard a beautiful goose—the finest goose Mrs. Goddard had ever seen.”
bcc49c6dd00d: What is Bacon's main claim in the first sentence?
Indoor, delicate trades weaken a warlike spirit
Indoor arts make nations richer and braver
He states that “sedentary, and within-door arts, and delicate manufactures... have, in their nature, a contrariety to a military disposition.”
What does “travail” most nearly mean in this passage?
Warlike people “are a little idle, and love danger better than travail,” contrasting danger with steady labour.
What solution does Bacon propose once slavery has been abolished?
Leave delicate trades to foreigners and keep natives in strong trades
He suggests “to leave those arts chiefly to strangers” and keep the natives as “tillers of the ground; free servants; and handicraftsmen of strong and manly arts.”
713832127e08: What is Emerson's central idea in this passage?
Self-reliance is the measure of reality and goodness
Commerce is the highest human virtue
War is the source of all truth
He says self-existence “constitutes the measure of good,” and nature shows “the self-sufficing and therefore self-relying soul.”
How does Emerson use nature to support his claim?
He gives examples of things that sustain themselves
He describes nature's beauty for its own sake
He argues nature is weak without people
He lists dangerous animals to avoid
He cites “the bended tree recovering itself from the strong wind” as a demonstration of self-reliance.
What does “Nature suffers nothing to remain in her kingdoms which cannot help itself” mean?
Nature does not let things survive unless they can sustain themselves
Nature feels pain for every creature
Nature has many kingdoms ruled by kings
Here “suffers” means allows, linked to the claim that “Power is, in nature, the essential measure of right.”
860a4d055bde: Why did Martha keep the children in?
She thought they had been naughty
“Martha thought it was naughtiness, and not misfortune.”
How does the narrator feel about Martha?
The narrator understands her and asks readers not to blame her
The narrator thinks she is cruel
The narrator is afraid of her
The narrator says “you must not blame her. She only thought she was doing her duty.”
What does the narrator say about grown-ups who punish children?
They often really are sorry to do it
They forget why they did it
Grown-ups say “it hurts them as much as it hurts you - and this is really very often the truth.”
c2b282b7c48f: How does the letter from Clerval affect the narrator?
It revives him and makes him decide to leave
It makes him angry and upset
It makes him want to stay forever
“This letter in a degree recalled me to life, and I determined to quit my island at the expiration of two days.”
What does the phrase “recalled me to life” suggest about the narrator's state on the island?
He had been withdrawn and lifeless in spirit
He had been too busy to think
The letter “in a degree recalled me to life,” implying he had been sunk in gloom on his “solitary isle.”
Why does Clerval want the narrator to join him soon?
He may soon leave on a longer voyage
He is ill and needs care
He has lost all his money
He wants to live on the island
His journey “might be followed, even sooner than he now conjectured, by his longer voyage,” so he wants the narrator's company.
dceb1e4e4b0d: What is the tone of Pip's description of Trabb's boy?
Mock-serious, exaggerating his outrage for humour
Pip says nothing less than “his heart’s best blood” would satisfy him, an exaggeration that is comic.
What does the metaphor “an invulnerable and dodging serpent” suggest about the boy?
He was slippery and impossible to catch or punish
The boy, “when chased into a corner, flew out again between his captor’s legs, scornfully yelping.”
What does Pip's letter to Mr. Trabb reveal about Pip?
He responds with pompous, wounded pride
He wants to hire the boy himself
He is afraid of Mr. Trabb
He writes that “Mr. Pip must decline to deal further” with anyone employing a boy who excited “Loathing in every respectable mind.”
ecc1abdcb8f5: Why are the Blefuscudians at first “confounded with astonishment”?
They do not understand what Gulliver plans to do
They have never seen ships before
They “had not the least imagination of what I intended,” thinking he only meant “to let the ships run adrift.”
What causes their “scream of grief and despair”?
Realizing Gulliver is towing away their whole fleet
Hearing that Lilliput has won the war
They scream “when they perceived the whole fleet moving in order, and saw me pulling at the end.”
What does Gulliver's calm treatment of his wounds suggest about his size?
The arrows are tiny and only a minor nuisance to him
He is badly injured and near death
He is the same size as the Blefuscudians
He fears the arrows more than the sea
He merely “stopped awhile to pick out the arrows that stuck in my hands and face” and walks on with his cargo.
ecedbbfeb11c: Why does the boy jump up when Heidi draws the zigzag roof?
He recognizes the landmark and knows the way
He is frightened by her finger
He wants to play a game
He is late for his supper
“he was evidently in the habit of guiding himself by similar landmarks,” so he “ran straight off.”
What does Sebastian's hurried “Make haste!” suggest?
People at the house have been worried or waiting for Heidi
Sebastian is angry with the boy
He opens “quickly” and cries “in a hurried voice,” showing urgency about her return.
How does Heidi describe her home to the boy?
By describing a large grey house with a zigzag roof
By telling him the street name
By naming the people who live there
She says “you can see a very, very large grey house, and the roof runs like this,” drawing “a zigzag line in the air.”
34f0696282f1: What does the narrator's firm instruction to Adèle reveal about her role?
She is responsible for keeping the child out of the guests' way
She is the lady of the house
She is a guest at the party
She tells Adèle “she must not on any account think of venturing in sight of the ladies... unless expressly sent for.”
What does the phrase “ladies’ silvery accents” suggest?
The women's voices sound light, bright and elegant
The women are wearing silver jewellery
The women speak with foreign accents
The women are angry and shrill
The description of “gentlemen’s deep tones and ladies’ silvery accents” blending “harmoniously” portrays a refined, cheerful sound.
How does the narrator experience the arrival of the guests?
From a distance, hearing more than seeing
As the main hostess greeting everyone
As a guest dancing in the hall
Through a letter describing it later
She “lost sight of” the cavalcade and then notes only that “A joyous stir was now audible in the hall.”
765c1ed4546b: What are Stickly-Prickly and Slow-Solid doing in this passage?
Stickly-Prickly practices “that side-stroke,” while Slow-Solid tries “that fascinating bend.”
What does Slow-Solid mean by “a regular whale”?
After Stickly-Prickly practices swimming, Slow-Solid says “A little more practice will make you a regular whale.”
Why do the two animals want to learn these tricks?
Slow-Solid says, “Won’t Painted Jaguar be surprised!”
e3308ea30255: Why were the soldiers less watchful?
They were sleepy in the hot afternoon
The soldiers were “somewhat sleepy with the sultriness of the afternoon” and “stood dozing at their posts.”
What does the hyperbole “a hundred eyes in every part of him” emphasize?
How much constant watchfulness the escape required
That the narrator could see very well
That the valley was full of animals
He says “A man had need of a hundred eyes in every part of him, to keep concealed in that uneven country.”
Why did the travellers have to judge “the solidity of every stone”?
Any rolling pebble would make a loud noise
The ground was covered in ice
In the still air “the rolling of a pebble sounded abroad like a pistol shot.”
d24e62aabf98: What does the metaphor “a mighty graveyard” convey about the city?
Death and emptiness had overwhelmed it
It was a quiet, peaceful place
“The city was become a mighty graveyard, two-thirds of the population had deserted the place.”
Why were the poor, the aged and the sick left behind?
They could not flee like the others
They were immune to the fever
They were hired to guard the city
They wanted to care for the stores
Only they “remained behind, a sure prey for the insidious enemy,” while two-thirds of the people had gone.
What is the effect of the sentence “A slight indisposition, then an hour of fever, then the hideous delirium, then—the Yellow Death!”?
Its rapid sequence shows how quickly the disease killed
It explains how to cure the fever
It shows the disease took years
It describes a doctor's daily routine
The quick steps support the claim that “In the briefest space it struck down and swept away even the most vigorous victim.”
f73513c3c628: What is Leacock's real purpose in this essay opening?
To amuse by treating clothing troubles like serious diseases
To sell new suits of clothes
He proposes that “The diseases of the clothes may roughly be divided into medical cases and surgical cases,” a comic mock-scientific idea.
What does the word “habiliments” mean here?
He speaks of “the powerful influence of the habiliments in their reaction upon the wearer,” referring to the clothes in the proverb.
How does Leacock create humour in “the haunted face of one suffering from internal loss of buttons”?
He uses grand medical language for a trivial problem
He tells a sad true event
Words like “haunted” and “suffering” are applied to the minor problem of “internal loss of buttons.”
bbecd2bf3212: How do Meg's and Amy's advice differ?
Meg values the story's ideas; Amy values selling the book
Meg wants it shorter; Amy wants it longer
Both want Jo to stop writing
Meg cares about money; Amy cares about art
Meg says “the interest of the story is more in the minds,” but Amy says “He knows what will sell.”
What does the word “digress” most nearly mean in Amy's advice?
Wander from the main story into side topics
Amy says once Jo has a name she “can afford to digress, and have philosophical and metaphysical people.”
What does the narrator's comment about Meg suggest?
Meg's opinion is shaped by loving admiration for Jo's book
Meg “firmly believed that this book was the most remarkable novel ever written,” so she is hardly neutral.
bda9b77ce745: What does the phrase “One side of the shield” suggest Messner is doing?
Pointing out that there is another view of the man
Describing a real piece of armour
He speaks “with an air of weighing the matter judicially” and then gives the other side's opinion.
What overall impression of the man does Messner give?
A man of some talent whose career was ruined
He “had some talent” and was “slated for the head of the English department,” but “It quite broke his career.”
What does Messner suggest hurt the man most?
Something involving his wife, whom he cared for
Messner says it was “a knock-out blow to him. It was thought he cared a great deal for his wife.”
11bdd5bfa2c4: What does Marcus Aurelius treat as truly good?
Virtues such as prudence, temperance, justice and fortitude
He names things “really good indeed, such as are prudence, temperance, justice, fortitude.”
What test does he use to separate true goods from false ones?
How people react when each is called good
When virtues are called good one “cannot endure to hear of any more,” but with what “the vulgar” esteem, “he doth hearken for more.”
What is the tone of the final question about wealth?
Ironic, mocking the idea that riches are truly good
He asks whether those so rich they lack a place of their own “ought not also in very deed to be much respected,” a sarcastic challenge.
dc0637e011fb: What does Rosamond's silence and playing with her reticule show?
She quietly intends to do as she likes anyway
She agrees fully with her aunt
She is too shy to understand
“She was not a fiery young lady and had no sharp answers, but she meant to live as she pleased.”
Why is Rosamond's pride hurt by her aunt's question?
She cannot say Lydgate has actually proposed
She “did not like being unable to say Yes” when asked whether Lydgate “has really made you an offer.”
What does “her habitual control of manner” suggest about Rosamond?
She is practised at hiding her feelings
Though “Her pride was hurt,” her “habitual control of manner helped her” keep composed.
3949c5309919: Why does the hunter want Muir to take Carlo?
He fears the summer heat on the plains could kill the dog
He no longer wants the dog
He wants Muir to sell him
He “feared that if he were compelled to stay all summer on the plains the fierce heat might be the death of him.”
What impression does Muir give of Carlo?
An intelligent dog who seems to understand people
A lazy pet who sleeps a lot
Carlo looked at him “with eyes expressing wonderful intelligence” and followed “as if he perfectly understood.”
What does Carlo's waiting for his master's wave show?
His wish to stay on the plains
He went with Muir only “after permission was given by a wave of the hand toward me and a farewell patting caress.”
c9efd57a419f: What mood do the Sunday breakfasts create?
They were “delightful Sunday breakfasts,” with sunlight “making everything on the table shine and glitter.”
How do Lena's feelings toward Prince change?
She goes from not wanting him to growing fond of him
She loves him at first and then dislikes him
She fears him more and more
“at first she was not at all pleased,” but “Prince was a knowing little beast, and she grew fond of him.”
Why does Prince's “gravity” make them laugh?
His serious look contrasts with the silly costume and pose
Wearing a “cadet cap” and holding a “yard-measure,” his solemn air was comic: “His gravity made us laugh immoderately.”
5e429446fa88: Why did Douglass seldom speak at anti-slavery meetings?
He felt others said what he wanted to say much better
He was not allowed to attend
He did not care about the cause
He writes, “what I wanted to say was said so much better by others.”
What does Douglass mean by calling speaking “a severe cross”?
It was a heavy, painful burden for him
“It was a severe cross, and I took it up reluctantly,” because “the idea of speaking to white people weighed me down.”
How does Douglass's feeling change once he begins to speak?
He moves from feeling enslaved to feeling free
He grows more frightened and stops
He becomes angry with the audience
He “felt myself a slave,” but after a few moments “I felt a degree of freedom, and said what I desired with considerable ease.”
a320e7229730: What does Winston conclude about the little man?
He is always playing a part out of fear
He is relaxed and has nothing to hide
Winston thinks “the man's whole life was playing a part, and that he felt it to be dangerous to drop his assumed personality.”
What does Julia's reaction to the wine suggest?
Wine is something rare and unfamiliar to her
She is afraid of being poisoned
She sniffs her glass “with frank curiosity,” and Winston recalls such a drink only from “dim memories.”
What does the simile “gleamed like a ruby” emphasize?
The rich, precious-looking colour of the wine
“Seen from the top the stuff looked almost black, but in the decanter it gleamed like a ruby.”
2f8e2bbc9ce7: Why does Sikes think Oliver's rescuers will not look for him?
They fear having to prosecute him
They’ll “ask no questions after him, fear they should be obliged to prosecute, and so get him lagged.”
What does Oliver's sudden flight show about his feelings?
He is horrified and desperate to escape
He is excited to see his friends
He wants to fetch the books
He “tore wildly from the room: uttering shrieks for help, which made the bare old house echo to the roof.”
What does Nancy's action reveal about her?
She tries to protect Oliver from harm
She springs before the door, crying, “Keep back the dog; he’ll tear the boy to pieces.”
135495cd806e: What is the main point of this passage?
Rudimentary organs are undeveloped forms of full organs
Rudimentary organs have no connection to real organs
Darwin concludes that “the rudiment and the perfect pistil are essentially alike in nature.”
How does the beetle example support Darwin's claim?
Closely similar beetles show both full wings and wing rudiments
Beetles with no wings fly fastest
Beetles grow wings when crossed with plants
One beetle has “full-sized wings, and another mere rudiments of membrane,” so “the rudiments represent wings.”
What does “retain their potentiality” mean here?
Keep the ability to develop fully
Such organs “are merely not developed,” and cows' extra teats “sometimes become developed and give milk.”
20f8080ed59d: How does Anne feel when Captain Wentworth seems to look away?
Disappointed that she was a moment too late
Relieved he did not see her
“It seemed as if she had been one moment too late,” and “she would rather have caught his eye.”
What does the phrase “forced to seem to restore her attention” suggest?
She must hide her real interest and pretend to watch the orchestra
She truly enjoys the music more
She is bored by Captain Wentworth
She has lost her place in the programme
She is “forced to seem to restore her attention to the orchestra,” though her thoughts are on him.
How does Anne feel about Mr Elliot at this moment?
She is eager to talk with him
She hopes he will introduce her
“She had no longer any inclination to talk to him. She wished him not so near her.”
642ebba946dc: Why do the cheers “not come” when Peter returns?
The boys are upset about something they fear to tell him
Tootles drops on his knees and others cry “Oh, mournful day,” showing grief.
How does Peter's mood change in the passage?
From proud excitement to growing worry
He arrives with “glorious tidings” but soon asks “Have you not seen her?” while “becoming troubled.”
What does Tootles show by offering to show Peter?
Courage to face Peter with the truth
When the others would hide her, Tootles says “quietly” that he will show her: “Back, twins, let Peter see.”
cc30ef6c4391: Why is Aunt Polly “too dazed to say more”?
Pollyanna's reasoning surprises and confuses her
She has fallen and hurt herself
Pollyanna's argument that not banging doors means “you weren't ever glad over anything” leaves her stunned.
What is Pollyanna's logic about banging doors?
People bang doors when they are glad
She says, “if you'd felt like banging doors you'd have banged 'em,” or else you were never glad.
What does the last sentence suggest about Miss Polly?
Pollyanna's words have made her question herself
She is planning to punish Pollyanna
Miss Polly “felt vaguely disturbed” and insists to herself she “HAD been glad—over some things!”
